title: Chicago's First Murder
premise: 17 June 1812, sunset, at the fort gate: the first killing written down in Chicago's history. The man who died was Jean Lalime, who spoke for the fort with its neighbors. The man who killed him was John Kinzie. Nine stops.

opening.text:
JAUNT: CHICAGO'S FIRST MURDER. Chicago in 1812 is a small, crowded place. There is a fort with about fifty soldiers and their leader, Captain Nathan Heald. There is a government trading house, and a few houses on the north side of the river. Everyone knows everyone. Two of these men have not gotten along for years. They argued over a house and over selling to the soldiers. They also argued over how to treat their neighbors, as a war with Britain came closer.

There are nine stops. We start with the sad ending. Then we go back to see how it happened. People told this story in three different ways. You will hear all three.

The story starts outside the gate of Fort Dearborn, at sunset on 17 June 1812.

stops.text: It is 17 June 1812, at sunset, outside the gate of Fort Dearborn. Jean Lalime lies still on the ground. He was the fort's interpreter. That means he helped people who spoke different languages understand each other. Lalime is dead. The man walking away, hurt in the shoulder, is John Kinzie. He is the trader who sells to the soldiers. Later, books would call him the Father of Chicago. Everyone agrees that Kinzie killed Lalime. But why he did it is still argued. To see how it came to this, go back eight years, across the river, to the best house in town.

stage.caption: Lalime lies where he fell; Kinzie walks away.

stops.text: It is May 1804, in the morning. This is the best house in Chicago. Jean Baptiste Point du Sable built it. He was the trader who settled here first. In 1800 he sold it. The paper for the sale says the buyer was Jean Lalime, using money from the man both Lalime and Kinzie worked for. John Kinzie signed that paper as a witness. Now Kinzie moves his own family in and makes the house his. Nobody has found any paper saying Lalime sold it to Kinzie. Lalime did not leave town. He moved a few doors west, close enough to watch Kinzie live in the house.

stage.caption: Watch the Kinzies move into the du Sable house, and Lalime look on from along the bank.

stops.text: It is 26 May 1811, in the afternoon. Years before, Lalime had spent a winter in the big house with the fort's first doctor. The doctor called him a very good man and a good friend. When Kinzie took the house, Lalime moved here, to a smaller house down the river bank. He became the fort's interpreter. Today he writes a letter to the governor in St. Louis. He passes on news that horses were stolen from farms to the south. A history writer said his letters show a smart, well-taught man. Across the river, something new is about to make Kinzie richer, and Lalime his enemy.

stage.caption: Lalime at his own door, writing to Governor Clark.

stops.text: It is 10 March 1812, in the morning, at the factory. This is the government's own trading house. Matthew Irwin runs it, and he sells things at fair prices. In January, Captain Heald let Kinzie and his partner be the only men allowed to sell goods to the soldiers. Today Irwin writes to the leaders in Washington. He says Kinzie and his partner offered money to get that job. Two men take Irwin's side: the young doctor, Isaac Van Voorhis, and Lalime. One army officer once wrote that Kinzie had a temper he could not control. Soon an argument about money turns into angry threats.

stage.caption: Irwin at his factory door with Van Voorhis and Lalime; Kinzie and Helm watching from the path.

stops.text: It is 16 April 1812, at the officers' rooms in the fort. Ten days ago, two farm workers were killed up the river. Now everyone is afraid. Irwin writes that some men at the fort said they wanted to harm their peaceful neighbors. He names Kinzie and Kinzie's son-in-law, Lieutenant Linai Helm. Ensign George Ronan, the youngest officer, threatens Lalime. Helm makes terrible threats against Irwin. In May, Captain Heald arrests Helm for planning to harm six Sauk men who came in peace. Then he lets him go. By June, everyone at the fort has picked a side.

stage.caption: Helm, Kinzie and Ronan talking hot; Ronan turns on Lalime as he passes with Irwin.

stops.text: It is 17 June 1812, about six in the evening, inside the fort. Tomorrow, far away in Washington, the country will go to war with Britain. The news will not get here for a month. On the open ground inside the fort, Helm shouts against Irwin's trading house. He says he wishes it would close. Kinzie takes his son-in-law's side. Lalime speaks up for Irwin's store. He says it is honest and fair. The voices get louder. Then Kinzie and Lalime walk out of the gate together. The gates will soon close for the night. Only one of the two men will walk back.

stage.caption: Watch the quarrel on the parade: Helm, then Lalime, then Kinzie; then Kinzie and Lalime walk out together.

stops.text: It is 17 June, at sunset, back outside the main gate. Victoire Porthier was a girl inside the fort. Years later she remembered it. It was sunset, when they shut the gates. She heard Helm call out to Kinzie to watch out, because Lalime had a pistol. Then she heard the pistol go off and saw the smoke. The two men fell down together. Kinzie got up, hurt in the shoulder. Lalime did not get up. Irwin saw it all from close by. The doctor said Kinzie had planned it. Kinzie's family said he was only defending himself.

stage.caption: Watch Kinzie and Lalime outside the gate at sunset, and what is left when it is over.

stops.text: It is 17 June, late at night. Irwin said one officer told Kinzie to run. He said Helm hid Kinzie in the fort for hours, then walked him to the river, shook his hand and let him go. Kinzie's family told it another way. They said he came home and his wife took him into the woods. She cared for his wound and hid him for days. Victoire said her father took Kinzie away to Milwaukee that night. That is three stories about one night. At the gate, Lalime still lies where he fell.

stage.caption: In the dark: Helm walks Kinzie down to the water, shakes his hand, and lets him go across the river in his own pirogue.

stops.text: It is 18 June, in the morning. The townspeople want a public meeting to find out how Lalime died. But Irwin wrote that Helm and a group of soldiers took Lalime's body away instead. They buried him on this bank, near the Kinzie house, inside a little fence. He could be seen from the house he had once owned on paper. In 1891, workers digging under a building found an old wooden coffin with bones inside. The bones went to the Chicago Historical Society.

stage.caption: Watch four of Helm's soldiers carry Lalime to his grave on a bier, while the townspeople who wanted an inquest look on.

legs.note: Eight years back, and across the river: this leg goes Instantly.

legs.story: Walk a few steps west along the bank, past Ouilmette's house.

legs.note: Across the river: there is no bridge in 1812. Fly, or go Instantly.

legs.story: Go through the main gate into the fort, to the officers' rooms.
Two months later, on the same open ground.
Go out through the main gate, the way the two men went.

legs.note: Across the river to the Kinzie house.
legs.story: Kinzie crosses the river in the dark.
Walk west along the bank, past Ouilmette's and Lalime's own house.

endings.text:
That night Captain Heald told Irwin to help arrest Kinzie. Irwin would not help, so he was sent out of the fort. Later Heald wrote that Kinzie had killed a man right in front of Irwin. Irwin left in July and was taken prisoner by the British. The doctor, Van Voorhis, died that August. Kinzie lived. He came back in 1816, and his family told their side of the story for a hundred years.

So was it murder? People who study history still disagree.

Some say Kinzie was guilty. Irwin and the doctor said Kinzie was behind a lot of dishonest dealing at the fort. A newspaper in 2018 said the story that Kinzie was only defending himself was not true.

Some say Kinzie was not to blame. His family said Lalime was jealous and attacked first. One book says the officers decided the killing was not a crime. Victoire said Kinzie was not to blame. Then she added, that is what they all said.

For a long time, only the story told by Kinzie's family and friends got heard. Lalime's bones are still in a box at the Chicago History Museum. You have stood where he fell. Decide for yourself.

keepsake.title: Quaife's verdict on the Lalime killing, 1913
keepsake.text: In 1913 a history writer named Milo Quaife decided this: it is clear that Kinzie killed Lalime, but from what we know, nobody can say who was to blame.

evidence.text: The Chicago Reader (2018) calls Lalime 'Chicago's first murder victim', 'a French interpreter who was stabbed to death in broad daylight and cold blood by the man that a century's worth of history books would call a founding father of the city of Chicago.' The killings at Hardscrabble in April came first, but 'since it wasn't Chicago at the time, Lalime is still considered the city's first murder victim.' Currey (1912): 'John Kinzie has been called "The Father of Chicago," and also "Chicago's Pioneer."' His granddaughter's 1910 book was titled John Kinzie, the Father of Chicago. Quaife (1913) disagreed: 'The propriety of designating Kinzie the "father of Chicago" is dubious.'
evidence.locator: Chicago Reader, 18 October 2018, the paragraphs beginning 'In an undisclosed location', 'Jean Lalime's journey' and 'In April 1812'; Currey ch. II, the paragraph beginning 'John Kinzie has been called'; Quaife, the paragraph beginning 'The propriety of designating Kinzie'

evidence.text: The Chicago Reader (2018) on the land record: 'The Wayne County Register of Deeds in Detroit ... Their records show Lalime, not Le Mai, bought Du Sable's trading post in 1800, bankrolled by Lalime and Kinzie's mutual boss, fur trader William Burnett. It couldn't have been confusion; Kinzie signed as witness.' No archive it asked 'could find any record for this story of the next time the property changed hands'. 'So as not to contradict the prominent Kinzie family, a convention developed that "Lalime" was "Le Mai" misspelled.' Kinzie bought the land from the government as unclaimed land in 1830.
evidence.locator: Chicago Reader, 18 October 2018, the paragraphs beginning 'The Wayne County Register of Deeds', 'Neither Wayne County' and 'So as not to contradict'

evidence.text: The family's version. Wau-Bun (1856): du Sable's improvements 'were taken possession of by a Frenchman named Le Mai', and 'After a few years Le Mai's establishment was purchased by John Kinzie, Esq.' Currey (1912): Le Mai 'occupied the house until 1804, when he in turn sold it to John Kinzie, who arrived with his family at Chicago in the fall of that year.' Quaife (1913) still has the house 'occupied by Le Mai, who had bought out Du Sable'.
evidence.locator: Wau-Bun ch. XVII (Gutenberg #12183); Currey ch. II, before the plate 'Residence of John Kinzie'; Quaife, the chapter on the first settlers (Gutenberg #69274)

evidence.text: Quaife (1913): when the troops came in 1803 the fourth house 'apparently, belonged to Kinzie and was at this time vacant. Doctor Smith, the first surgeon at Fort Dearborn, and John La Lime shortly secured possession of it for the winter and fitted it up in a comfortable manner for their joint occupancy.' 'The fourth name entered in Kinzie's account book after his removal to Chicago in May, 1804, is that of La Lime.' Dr. Smith called La Lime 'a very decent man and a good companion.' By 1808 'La Lime was living in one of the four houses on the north side of the river and acting as government Indian interpreter.' Jouett, the agent, named a son after him.
evidence.locator: Quaife, the chapter on the first settlers (Gutenberg #69274 plain text, the paragraphs on Fettle and on La Lime and Nash)

evidence.text: Lalime's own letters (Kirkland 1893): to Governor Clark, 26 May 1811, 'An Indian from the Peorias passed here yesterday and has given me information that the Indians about that place have been about the settlements of Kaskasia and Vincennes and have stolen from fifteen to twenty horses'; to John Johnson, 7 July 1811, of 'depredations and murders committed about the settlement of Cahokia'. Kirkland: the letters 'show that he was a man of ability and education', and an 1821 treaty reserved land for 'John B. Lalime, son of Noke-no-qua.'
evidence.locator: Appendix F, 'The Bones of John Lalime', Project Gutenberg eBook #59624 plain text lines 6120-6540

evidence.text: The Chicago Reader (2018): 'on January 17, 1812, Whistler's replacement, Captain Nathan Heald, issued a garrison order making "Messrs. Kinzie & Forsyth" the exclusive fort sutlers.' The factor, Matthew Irwin, ran the government's trading house; the sutler sold to the soldiers. Irwin's letter of 10 March, as the Reader quotes it: he had 'lately ascertained it to be an absolute fact that Messrs. Kinzie & Forsyth, offered a gentleman 400$ per annum to get them appointed at Washington the Suttlers for this place.' 'Irwin found two allies as horrified by the sutler contract as he was: surgeon's mate Dr. Isaac Van Voorhis and fort interpreter Jean Lalime.' Quaife (1913) gives the older feud: in 1810 Kinzie and Irwin had stood together against Captain Whistler over the garrison trade, and Cooper 'described the trader as a man of ungovernable temper, who frequently engaged in bitter quarrels.'
evidence.locator: Chicago Reader, 18 October 2018, the paragraphs beginning 'Just over two years later' to 'Irwin detailed'; Quaife, the 1810 feud

evidence.text: Irwin to the War Department, 16 April 1812, as the Chicago Reader quotes it, after the killings at Lee's Place: 'Propositions were openly made to murder them as well as some French persons (with Indian wives) who have, ever since they have been here, manifested peaceable dispositions,' and 'The principal persons who advised & insisted upon such measures being carried into effect, were the Suttler for this garrison & his Son-in law—Lt Helm.' The Reader: 'Ronan threatened to shoot Lalime and Helm "swore 'he would take the Scalp of the Factor'"'; and 'Heald did arrest Helm in May for plotting to murder six Sauk who had come to the fort in peace', releasing him 'after he apologized.'
evidence.locator: Chicago Reader, 18 October 2018, the paragraphs beginning 'In April 1812' to 'Kinzie was behind it all'

evidence.text: Van Voorhis to the War Department, 30 June 1812, as the Chicago Reader tells and quotes it: on 17 June, around 6 p.m., inside the fort, Helm went on a tirade about Irwin, 'concluding ... by saying he would give a very handsome treat if the Factory would be done away!' Kinzie took his son-in-law's side. '[T]he unfortunate Interpreter defended the pure motives and just dealings of the Institution,' Van Voorhis wrote (the Reader prints 'lnstitution').
evidence.locator: Chicago Reader, 18 October 2018, the paragraphs beginning 'The situation reached a head' and '[T]he unfortunate Interpreter'

evidence.text: Victoire Porthier, a girl inside the fort, as Andreas printed her and Kirkland reprints: 'My sister Madeline and I saw the fight between John Kinzie and Lalime, when Lalime was killed. It was sunset, when they used to shut the gates of the fort. Kinzie and Lalime came out together, and soon we heard Lieutenant Helm call out for Mr. Kinzie to look out for Lalime, as he had a pistol. Quick we saw the men come together. We heard the pistol go off and saw the smoke. Then they fell down together. I don't know as Lalime got up at all, but Kinzie got home pretty quick. Blood was running from his shoulder, where Lalime had shot him. In the night he packed up some things and my father took him to Milwaukee'. 'I don't know what the quarrel was about. It was an old one--business, I guess.'
evidence.locator: Appendix F, 'The Bones of John Lalime', Project Gutenberg eBook #59624 plain text lines 6120-6540, Mrs. Porthier's statement

evidence.text: Gurdon Hubbard to John Wentworth, 25 June 1881, giving what Mrs. Kinzie and Mrs. Helm told him (Kirkland 1893): 'Lalime met him outside the garrison and shot him, the ball cutting the side of his neck.' 'Mr. Kinzie, closing with Lalime, stabbed him and returned to the house covered with blood.' His wife 'with him retreated to the woods, where as soon as possible she dressed his wounds'. 'For several days he was hid in the bush and cared for by his wife.' Lalime 'should be buried near Kinzie's house, in plain view from his front door and piazza. The grave was enclosed in a picket fence'. Hubbard believed Kinzie acted 'in self-defence', and that the officers 'acquitted Mr. Kinzie'.
evidence.locator: Appendix F, 'The Bones of John Lalime', Project Gutenberg eBook #59624 plain text lines 6120-6540, Hubbard's letter

evidence.text: The Chicago Reader (2018), from Irwin's report: 'Kinzie saw that Irwin had seen the whole thing from 20 to 30 yards away, and called out that he was a "lost man"'; 'Ronan told Kinzie to run. Helm helped Kinzie. Heald did nothing.' Van Voorhis, 30 June 1812: 'suffice it to say that it was a perfect assassination and can be proven to be such'. 'After the murder, Kinzie hid in the fort garrison for about four hours, until Lieutenant Helm walked him to the river's edge, shook his hand, and let the future father of Chicago run free.' A sentinel later saw Helm carrying him food and wine.
evidence.locator: Chicago Reader, 18 October 2018, the paragraphs beginning 'A knife came out', 'I need not trouble you', 'Lalime's body lay' and 'Although Kinzie was seen'

evidence.text: Irwin, July 1812, as the Chicago Reader quotes him: 'The Citizens were anxious an inquest should be held in the body, but a file of soldiers headed by Lt. Helm carried it away by force.' Kirkland (1893) puts the fenced grave, by Hubbard's account, 'two hundred yards west of the Kinzie house'. Fernando Jones, who came in 1835, saw 'a grave situated a little to the north of our path and several hundred feet west of the Kinzie house. The grave was surrounded by a neat white picket fence.' On 29 April 1891 cellar diggers at the south-west corner of Cass and Illinois streets found a skeleton and 'fragments, nearly crumbled away, of a rude pine coffin'; Kirkland gave the bones to the Chicago Historical Society.
evidence.locator: Chicago Reader, 18 October 2018, the paragraph beginning 'Irwin never said anything about the grave'; Kirkland Appendix F, 'The Bones of John Lalime', Project Gutenberg eBook #59624 plain text lines 6120-6540

evidence.text: This stand is about 180 m, Hubbard's 'two hundred yards', west of the Kinzie house on the north bank, looking back east along the bank to the houses; it marks the distance he gave, not a found grave.
evidence.reasoning: Hubbard's figure through Kirkland, Appendix F; Fernando Jones has 'several hundred feet west'. The anchor west_of_kinzie_house is a camera, not a claim of the grave's place.

evidence.text: Heald to Irwin, as the Chicago Reader quotes him: 'be good enough to inform him that it was in Consequence of your refusing to obey my orders when Called on to assist in apprehending a Citizen who had but a few days previous stabed an other citizen to the heart in your presence'. 'Irwin left Fort Dearborn on July 5 to hire a new interpreter. He arrived at Fort Mackinac just in time to become a British prisoner of war.' Irwin on 12 October: 'if he fulfilled his part as emissary, he had it much in his power to preserve his own life by destroying the Witnesses to the murder of Lalime.' Van Voorhis died in the attack of 15 August (Heald's report). Quaife (1913): 'The fact of La Lime's death at the hands of Kinzie is clear; the responsibility for it cannot, in the light of existing information, be determined.' The bones are kept by the Chicago History Museum in off-site storage (the Reader).
evidence.locator: Chicago Reader, 18 October 2018, the paragraphs beginning 'And, when you report', 'Irwin left Fort Dearborn', 'The plots entered into' and the opening paragraphs; Quaife, the paragraph on La Lime's death

evidence.text: Captain Nathan Heald, writing from Chicago on 15 April 1812: 'On the 6th instant, a little before sunset, a party of eleven Indians, supposed to be Winnebagoes, came to Messrs. Russell and Lee's cabin, in a field on the Portage branch of the Chicago river, about three miles from the garrison, where they murdered two men, one by the name of Liberty White, an American, and the other a Canadian Frenchman whose name I do not know.' The 1895 editors add the name [Debou] in brackets.
evidence.locator: p. 43, data/research/books/text/moses_kirkland_history_of_chicago_v1.txt lines 6876-6890 (machine OCR of the 1895 printing, read as corrected: Heald's letter of 15 April 1812)

evidence.text: Stops that tell a record are set on its date: Kinzie's first season at Chicago (May 1804, the month his account book there begins), Lalime's letter of 26 May 1811, Irwin's letters of 10 March and 16 April 1812, and the morning after the killing. The hours of those stops are the jaunt's, chosen for daylight; no source gives them.
evidence.reasoning: Each date is the date of the document the stop tells; the hours are pacing, not records.

evidence.text: Sunset at the gate, then 'about four hours' hidden in the garrison before Helm walked Kinzie to the river: this stop is set at twenty past eleven that night. Porthier says only 'In the night'.
evidence.reasoning: The Reader's 'about four hours' from Irwin's report, counted from sunset on 17 June (about 7:20 local solar time at Chicago); an estimate.

evidence.text: Quaife (1913): 'Meanwhile war had been declared by Congress on June 18'. 'News of the declaration of war was received at Fort Dearborn toward the middle of July.'
evidence.locator: Quaife, the chapter on the evacuation (Gutenberg #69274 plain text, the paragraphs on Hull's march and on the news reaching Fort Dearborn)

evidence.text: The Chicago Reader (2018): 'The story of Lalime's 1812 murder at the hands of early settler John Kinzie is a popular lie'; the self-defence version was 'traced back to Kinzie's wife and one of their servants'. Irwin's and Van Voorhis's letters 'tell the story of three forgotten men who tried and failed to end the corruption, bribery, and smuggling that defined life at the fort that became Chicago.' 'Kinzie was behind it all, the doctor and factor alleged.' 'The winners didn't write the history books. The books ... were how the Kinzies made themselves the winners.' 'Cracks started to form in the story in the 20th century, when Quaife found a few of Irwin's letters'. Quaife, 1915, as the Reader quotes him: 'To those who subscribe to a traditional estimate local to Chicago which pictures Kinzie as a kind of demigod, Irwin's charge that in addition to being a murderer and a traitor he contrived the massacre of the garrison and settlers in order to destroy the witnesses of his crime will come as a distinct shock'. Porthier, as the Reader quotes her: 'You see Kinzie wasn't to blame at all.' 'That is what they all said.' Peter Alter of the Chicago History Museum: 'What I do know is that a lot is not known'.
evidence.locator: Chicago Reader, 18 October 2018, the paragraphs beginning 'The story of Lalime's 1812 murder', 'The real story', 'Kinzie was behind it all', 'The winners didn't', 'You see Kinzie', 'Cracks started to form', 'To those who subscribe' and 'What I do know'

evidence.text: Quaife (1913): 'La Lime's side of the story has not been preserved, except in the form of unreliable verbal tradition, which pictures Kinzie in the light of aggressor and murderer.' 'The Kinzie family tradition represents that La Lime, insanely jealous over Kinzie's success as a trader, treacherously attacked him, armed with a pistol and dirk, and was stabbed to death by Kinzie in self-defense. Practically all writers on Chicago history hitherto have accepted this version, but it is as little worthy of credence as the contrary one.' 'When in a later generation interest in his fate was revived only the version of it originating with the relatives and friends of the slayer gained the public ear, and this, for obvious reasons, put the onus of the affray on the slain.'
evidence.locator: Quaife, the paragraph beginning 'In the summer of 1812, a few weeks before the massacre' (Gutenberg #69274 plain text)

evidence.text: Currey (1912): 'An inquiry into all the circumstances of the affair was made by the officers of the garrison, and a verdict of justifiable homicide was reached.' 'It was said by Gurdon S. Hubbard in later years that Mr. Kinzie deeply regretted the killing of Lalime, and further, that he firmly believed the deed was committed in self-defence.'
evidence.locator: Currey ch. II, the paragraphs beginning 'An inquiry into all the circumstances' and 'It was said by Gurdon S. Hubbard'
